t1_mistake_agree.hook: ✗ Don't say this / at work: “I am agree.”
t1_mistake_agree.reviewer: Claude (expert American English teacher review, 26/10/2026 rewrite for engagement; no GrabCast)

script.m_s: It feels like: I am happy. I am tired.
script.m_y: But agree is an action, like want or need.
script.m_k: Drop the am. Just say: I agree.
script.m_x: I don't agree. Do you agree?
script.m_t: Sound like a native: I couldn't agree more!
script.m_q: Quick quiz! Which one is right?
script.m_c: Save this, and check your grammar on lexkite.com.

t1_mistake_agree.note: “I am agree” is a very common learner error (agree is a verb; learners copy be + adjective like happy/tired). Fix: I agree / I don't agree / Do you agree? Native upgrade “I couldn't agree more” = strong agreement, natural US/UK. Hook 'at work' is true: it is a frequent meeting phrase and sounds non-native.

t4_pair_borrow_lend.reviewer: Claude (expert American English teacher review, 26/10/2026 series rewrite for engagement; no GrabCast)

script.p_h: Borrow or lend? Don't mix them up.
script.p_s: You need a pen. Your friend has one.
script.p_b: Borrow means you take it, then give it back.
script.p_l: Lend means you give it, and get it back.
script.p_l2: Sure! I can lend you my pen.
script.p_t: Easy trick: borrow from, lend to.
script.p_q: Quiz! My brother blank me ten dollars.
script.p_a: Lent! My brother lent me ten dollars.
script.p_c: Save this, and compare tricky words on lexkite.com.

t4_pair_borrow_lend.note: Borrow = receive temporarily (borrow FROM); lend = give temporarily (lend TO). 'My brother lent me $10' is correct; 'borrowed me' is a common learner error. The 'from/to' trick is standard teacher practice.

t5_roleplay_checkin.hook: ✈️ AIRPORT CHECK-IN / What do you say?
t5_roleplay_checkin.reviewer: Claude (expert American English teacher review, 25/10/2026; no GrabCast)

script.r_h: Airport check-in. Here's what to say.
script.r_1: Hi! Can I see your passport, please?
script.r_3: Are you checking any bags today?
script.r_5: Your turn. Ask for a window seat.
script.r_6: Could I get a window seat, please?

t5_roleplay_checkin.note: Natural US airport check-in exchange (agent: passport, checking bags; traveler: here you go, just one). Your-turn prompt + model answer “Could I get a window seat, please?” is polite and idiomatic.

script.f_m: That sounds like a table you can sit on!
script.f_r: Only three beats. Stress the first one.
script.f_y: Your turn. Repeat after me: comfortable.
script.f_b: Same trick: vegetable has three beats, not four.
script.f_c: Save this, and practice pronunciation on lexkite.com.

t6_pron_comfortable.note: US /ˈkʌmftərbəl/ ~ /ˈkʌmftɚbəl/: 3 syllables in natural speech (COMF-ter-ble), stress on the first; 'com-for-TA-ble' is a common learner error. 'vegetable' /ˈvɛdʒtəbəl/ = 3 syllables (VEJ-tuh-ble) in natural US speech. The 'table' joke is about the learner form, not a claim.

t7_usuk_cookie.reviewer: Claude (expert American English teacher review, 26/10/2026 series rewrite for engagement; no GrabCast)

script.u_h: US or UK? Which word do you use?
script.u_s: You want a sweet snack with your coffee.
script.u_tw: Careful! In America, a biscuit is soft bread.
script.u_x: Can I have a cookie, please?
script.u_q: Quiz! You're in London. What do you ask for?
script.u_a: A biscuit! With tea, of course.
script.u_c: Save this, and compare tricky words on lexkite.com.

t7_usuk_cookie.note: US cookie = UK biscuit (sweet baked snack). In the US a 'biscuit' is a soft, scone-like quick bread (biscuits and gravy) – true surprise fact. In London you ask for a biscuit with tea.
